title: Care-management risk algorithm under-referred Black patients
organizations: Optum (developer); US health systems and insurers using the algorithm
what_happened: A 2019 Science study of a widely used commercial algorithm for selecting patients for care-management programs found that at the same risk score Black patients were considerably sicker than White patients. The authors estimated that fixing the disparity would raise the share of Black patients receiving extra help from 17.7% to 46.5%. Nature reported the algorithm helps manage care for about 200 million people in the US each year.
failure_mechanism: The model predicted future health care cost as a stand-in for health need, and less money is spent on Black patients with the same level of illness.
lesson_for_builders: Check what your target label actually measures; cost, utilization, or past decisions can encode unequal access rather than need.
outcome: Per Nature, Optum repeated the analysis, got the same results, and worked with the researchers on non-cost variables that reduced bias by 84%.
sources: Obermeyer et al., Science 2019 (abstract via Europe PMC); Nature news, Ledford, 24 Oct 2019
notes: Optum called the study's conclusion 'misleading' and said the cost model is one of many data elements used to select patients. The product name (Impact Pro) was not confirmed in a fetched source, so the row says Optum only.

title: Widely deployed sepsis model performed poorly in external validation
organizations: Epic Systems (developer); Michigan Medicine (validation site)
what_happened: An external validation at Michigan Medicine covering 38,455 hospitalizations found the Epic Sepsis Model had an AUROC of 0.63. It did not identify 1,709 of 2,552 patients with sepsis (67%) while alerting on 18% of all hospitalizations. The authors concluded the model had poor discrimination and calibration and raised concern about its widespread use.
failure_mechanism: A proprietary model deployed at many hospitals was not independently validated on local data before use, and its alert threshold produced many alerts while missing most cases.
lesson_for_builders: Validate on the deploying site's population and publish alert burden and sensitivity, not just AUC from development data.
sources: Wong et al., JAMA Intern Med 2021 (external validation of the Epic Sepsis Model)
notes: Single-site study. Epic's response was not found in a fetched source.

title: Lawsuit alleges algorithm drove post-acute care denials in Medicare Advantage
organizations: UnitedHealth Group; UnitedHealthcare; naviHealth
what_happened: A putative class action filed in 2023 (Estate of Lokken v. UnitedHealth Group, D. Minn.) alleges UnitedHealthcare used the nH Predict tool to deny Medicare Advantage members' post-acute care regardless of treating physicians' recommendations. Plaintiffs allege the company knew the tool was inaccurate because over 90% of denials that were appealed were reversed. On 13 February 2025 the court let the breach of contract and good faith claims proceed and dismissed most other claims as preempted; these allegations have not been decided.
failure_mechanism: Alleged reliance on a predictive length-of-stay estimate to set coverage limits instead of an individual clinical determination.
lesson_for_builders: If a model's output feeds coverage decisions, keep a clinician's individual review and an effective appeal path, and expect the model's use to be examined in discovery.
outcome: Pending: in discovery; a 9 March 2026 order compelled UnitedHealthcare to produce nH Predict analyses and related documents. No class certification or merits ruling found as of 2026-10-12.
sources: BankInfoSecurity, summary of the court ruling and allegations; DLA Piper, summary of the 13 Feb 2025 ruling; Arnall Golden Gregory, summary of the 2026 discovery order
notes: Allegations and the 13 Feb 2025 ruling are taken from law-firm and trade-press summaries of the court documents (primary filings not fetched). UnitedHealth disputes the claims. The Oct 2024 Senate PSI report on Medicare Advantage post-acute denials describes heavy automation at UnitedHealthcare, CVS, and Humana but is not cited because the fetched summary does not name nH Predict.

title: Reported batch claim denials by Cigna physicians using an automated flag
organizations: Cigna
what_happened: ProPublica and The Capitol Forum reported in March 2023, from internal records, that Cigna doctors denied over 300,000 claims in two months, spending an average of about 1.2 seconds per case, after software flagged claims whose diagnosis codes did not match approved tests. Cigna called the description incorrect and said the system was meant to speed approvals for routine screenings. A class action (Kisting-Leung v. Cigna, E.D. Cal.) alleges the practice breached plan terms requiring medical director review; the court let part of the case proceed on 31 March 2025.
failure_mechanism: A human sign-off step reportedly became a batch click-through on automated flags, so the review added no independent judgment.
lesson_for_builders: Design review steps so the reviewer can actually disagree: show the basis, limit batch approvals, and measure how often reviewers override the tool.
outcome: Pending: in discovery; trial was set for 30 November 2027 in a scheduling order seen in search results (not fetched).
sources: ProPublica / Capitol Forum, 25 Mar 2023; NFP summary of the 31 Mar 2025 court order
notes: Facts from ProPublica/Capitol Forum reporting on internal records and a summary of the 31 Mar 2025 court order (order not read directly). Whether PxDx is 'AI' is contested: reporting describes software matching diagnosis codes to approved procedures.

title: Eating-disorder chatbot reportedly gave weight-loss advice and was taken down
organizations: National Eating Disorders Association (NEDA); Cass (chatbot vendor)
what_happened: In 2023 an eating-disorder consultant said NEDA's Tessa chatbot recommended losing 1 to 2 pounds a week, eating no more than 2,000 calories a day, and keeping a daily deficit of 500 to 1,000 calories. Tessa had been built with preprogrammed responses, and the vendor Cass later added generative AI. NEDA took the chatbot down within hours of the screenshots being posted and attributed the problem to the company operating it; NEDA and Cass both apologized.
failure_mechanism: A vendor added generative responses to a previously scripted mental-health chatbot, and the change was not tested against harmful advice for the at-risk population.
lesson_for_builders: Treat adding generative AI to a scripted health chatbot as a new product: red-team it with the highest-risk users before release.
outcome: NEDA took Tessa offline; it had also closed its human-staffed helpline the month before.
sources: NPR, 8 Jun 2023 (station copy)
notes: Advice is documented by the tester's screenshots as reported by NPR, and the takedown and apologies are from the organizations; no regulator or court finding. Single news source fetched; NEDA's 'bad actors' remark from search snippets was not used.

title: Teen suicide lawsuits against companion chatbot maker settled
organizations: Character Technologies (Character.AI); Google; Noam Shazeer; Daniel De Freitas
what_happened: A 2024 wrongful-death suit (Garcia v. Character Technologies, M.D. Fla.) alleged a 14-year-old died by suicide after developing a close relationship with a Character.AI chatbot, that the platform lacked adequate safety measures, and that it did not respond adequately to his self-harm statements. In May 2025 the judge declined at the pleading stage to treat chatbot output as protected speech and let claims, including those against Google, proceed. In January 2026 the companies agreed to settle this and four similar cases; terms were not disclosed.
failure_mechanism: A relational chatbot open to minors kept emotionally intense, sometimes sexualized, conversations going without effective crisis detection or age safeguards, as alleged.
lesson_for_builders: If users can form attachments, build crisis escalation, age gating, and session limits before launch, not after harm.
outcome: Settlement in principle announced January 2026 across cases in Florida, Colorado, New York and Texas; terms confidential. Character.AI said it stopped open-ended chat for under-18 users in late 2025.
sources: CNN via KTVZ, 7 Jan 2026; AP via WUFT, 23 May 2025
notes: All factual claims about the chatbot's behavior are allegations. Searches suggested the Garcia case was dismissed after the parties reported settlement, with 90 days to finalize; finalization was not confirmed. Sources do not say whether any admission was made. Character.AI's statement: it has taken steps on teen safety; Google says it is a separate company.

title: Texas AG settlement over a clinical AI vendor's hallucination-rate claims
organizations: Pieces Technologies; Texas Attorney General
what_happened: In September 2024 the Texas Attorney General announced a settlement with Pieces Technologies, whose generative AI products summarize and draft clinical notes for hospital EMRs. The AG alleged Pieces made false or misleading statements about the accuracy of its products, including an advertised hallucination rate below 0.001% (under 1 per 100,000). Pieces agreed to stop misleading statements and to disclose how its accuracy metrics are defined and calculated.
failure_mechanism: Accuracy and hallucination metrics were marketed to hospitals without a validated, disclosed method behind them, as alleged.
lesson_for_builders: Only publish accuracy or safety figures you can document, define the metric and test set, and expect customers and regulators to ask.
outcome: Assurance of voluntary compliance with disclosure and marketing commitments; no monetary penalty reported.
sources: Baker Donelson client alert, 23 Sep 2024
notes: The AG's press release (HTTP 402) and Fierce Healthcare (403) could not be fetched; a law-firm summary was used. Search results report that Pieces denies wrongdoing; that was not in the fetched page. The no-penalty point comes from search results and is not in the row's what_happened.

title: Diabetic retinopathy AI struggled with real clinic conditions in Thailand
organizations: Google Health; Eleven clinics in Thailand
what_happened: A human-centered study at the CHI 2020 conference observed nurses using a deep learning diabetic retinopathy screening system across eleven clinics in Thailand. Google's write-up says the system could label blurry or dark images ungradable. The study found a tension between the model's image-quality thresholds and the imperfect, resource-limited clinic conditions, which affected performance, nurse workflow, and patient experience.
failure_mechanism: The model was developed on high-quality images and its quality thresholds did not fit real clinic lighting and workflow, so some patients could not be assessed or were sent for unnecessary referral.
lesson_for_builders: Pilot in the real environment and design the fallback path for inputs the model rejects.
outcome: Google changed the research protocol so eye specialists review ungradable images with patient records rather than automatically referring those patients.
sources: Beede et al., CHI 2020 (abstract on Google Research); Google blog, 'Healthcare AI systems that put people at the center'
notes: Qualitative study. A third-party blog cites a figure for share of images rejected; it was not confirmed in the paper or Google's post, so no number is given. The system also helped nurses identify positive screenings quickly, per Google.

title: Cancer treatment advisor reportedly gave unsafe recommendations
organizations: IBM Watson Health; Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center
what_happened: STAT reported in July 2018, citing internal IBM slide decks from 2017, that company specialists and customers had identified multiple examples of unsafe and incorrect treatment recommendations from Watson for Oncology while IBM was marketing it. The documents attributed the problems largely to training on a small number of synthetic (hypothetical) cases and to recommendations reflecting a few specialists' opinions rather than guidelines or evidence.
failure_mechanism: Training content built from hypothetical cases and a few experts' preferences rather than real patient data and guidelines.
lesson_for_builders: Train and test recommendation tools on real cases and current guidelines, and let users see the basis for each recommendation.
sources: STAT News, 25 Jul 2018 (visible portion, rest paywalled)
notes: Based on journalism about internal documents; no regulator or court finding. Part of the article is behind a paywall, and IBM's response and any statement on patient harm were not confirmed; claims here are limited to the visible text. Secondary coverage says IBM said it had learned and improved Watson Health from client feedback; not verified.

title: Dermatology AI models performed worse on dark skin tones
organizations: Authors of the Diverse Dermatology Images study (Daneshjou et al.)
what_happened: A 2022 Science Advances study released the Diverse Dermatology Images dataset, with pathologically confirmed images across skin tones. It found that state-of-the-art dermatology AI models performed substantially worse on the dataset, especially on dark skin tones and uncommon diseases, and that dermatologists who label training data also performed worse on dark skin tones and uncommon diseases. Fine-tuning on the diverse images narrowed the gap.
failure_mechanism: Training and benchmark image sets under-represented dark skin tones and uncommon diseases, so overall accuracy hid subgroup gaps.
lesson_for_builders: Report performance by skin tone and condition rarity, and build evaluation sets that include them.
sources: Daneshjou et al., Science Advances 2022 (abstract via Europe PMC)
notes: Numbers were not in the abstract that was fetched, so none are given.

title: Pulse oximeters more often missed low oxygen in Black patients
organizations: University of Michigan researchers (Sjoding et al.); Pulse oximeter manufacturers
what_happened: A 2020 NEJM letter compared pulse oximeter readings with arterial blood oxygen in two cohorts. Occult hypoxemia (arterial saturation below 88% despite a reading of 92 to 96%) occurred in 11.7% of measurements in Black patients versus 3.6% in White patients at Michigan, and 17.0% versus 6.2% in a 178-hospital ICU database. The authors concluded Black patients had roughly three times the rate of occult hypoxemia and that relying on oximetry to triage or adjust oxygen may put them at greater risk.
failure_mechanism: A sensor input was less accurate for darker skin, so downstream decisions and models built on it inherit the error.
lesson_for_builders: Check whether your input signals are equally accurate across groups before building a model or alert on them.
sources: Sjoding et al., NEJM 2020, vol 383, pp 2477-2478 (full text via PMC)
notes: Not an AI system: this is device measurement bias. Included because AI models that consume vital signs (sepsis, deterioration, triage) inherit it. Retrospective data.

title: Pneumonia detection CNN did worse at new hospitals and could identify the source hospital
organizations: Authors of the study (Zech et al.); NIH Clinical Center; Mount Sinai Hospital; Indiana University
what_happened: A 2018 PLOS Medicine study trained chest X-ray pneumonia models on data from Mount Sinai and the NIH Clinical Center and tested them at Indiana University. The best internal model had an AUC of 0.931, falling to 0.815 on the external Indiana data. The networks could identify the source hospital from the radiograph in over 99.9% of cases, and the authors said this hospital-level signal can confound predictions.
failure_mechanism: Models picked up site-specific signals, such as differences in pneumonia prevalence and image characteristics, instead of purely disease features.
lesson_for_builders: Test on data from a different site before claiming performance, and check whether the model can recover the site.
sources: Zech et al., PLOS Medicine 2018 (record via Europe PMC)
notes: Research models, not a deployed product.

title: Review found nearly all COVID-19 prediction models at high risk of bias
organizations: Authors of the BMJ living systematic review (Wynants et al.)
what_happened: A BMJ living systematic review screened 37,421 titles and appraised 232 COVID-19 diagnostic and prognostic prediction models from 169 studies. Every model was rated at high or unclear risk of bias, and only 11 (5%) were externally validated with a calibration plot. The authors concluded reported performance was probably optimistic and that unreliable predictions could cause more harm than benefit.
failure_mechanism: Models were built on small, non-representative samples with poor reporting and little external validation, so reported accuracy did not carry over.
lesson_for_builders: Follow reporting standards such as TRIPOD, validate externally, and treat early-pandemic-style rushed models with suspicion.
sources: Wynants et al., BMJ 2020, 369:m1328 (living review, record via Europe PMC)
notes: The record fetched reports update 3 of the living review; counts in earlier versions differ. A review of research models, not a single incident.

title: Speech-to-text model invented text, including harmful content
organizations: OpenAI (Whisper); Academic researchers (Koenecke et al.); Nabla (medical scribe vendor reported to build on Whisper)
what_happened: A peer-reviewed FAccT 2024 study found that roughly 1% of audio transcriptions by OpenAI's Whisper contained entire hallucinated phrases or sentences that were not in the audio, and 38% of those hallucinations included explicit harms such as violence, inaccurate associations, or false authority. Hallucinations occurred disproportionately for speakers with longer non-vocal stretches, a common symptom of aphasia.
failure_mechanism: A general-purpose speech model generated plausible text during silence or unclear audio instead of leaving a gap, and the original audio may not be kept for checking.
lesson_for_builders: Measure transcription hallucinations on your own recordings, flag low-confidence segments, keep a way to check the source audio, and require clinician review of AI-drafted notes.
sources: Koenecke et al., 'Careless Whisper' (arXiv 2402.08021, FAccT 2024)
notes: Study data were not clinical recordings. Press reports (Associated Press, Oct 2024) said medical scribe products built on Whisper were in clinical use and that one vendor deleted original audio; those reports could not be fetched and are not used in the row.

title: GPT-4 drafted patient-message replies sometimes judged unsafe if unedited
organizations: Authors of the Lancet Digital Health study (Chen et al.)
what_happened: A 2024 Lancet Digital Health study had physicians assess GPT-4 drafted replies to simulated patient messages. In 11 of 156 physician assessments (7.1%) the draft was judged to pose a risk of severe harm, and in one (0.6%) a risk of death, if left unedited. The authors said LLM drafts can sometimes cause serious harm if not edited and called for evaluation that reflects real clinical use.
failure_mechanism: The model produced fluent but clinically wrong or unsafe advice, and reviewers can overlook errors in fluent drafts.
lesson_for_builders: Test drafting tools for safety on realistic messages, and design the review step so clinicians actually check clinical content.
sources: Chen et al., Lancet Digital Health 2024 (PMC full text)
notes: Simulated scenarios, not live patient messages; an earlier preprint reported 7.7% for the same finding and the published 7.1% is used. A blog's claim that reviewers missed two-thirds of errors was not confirmed and is not used. The study was conducted in 2023 (setting not confirmed in the fetched page).

title: Mental-health peer support app tested GPT-3 replies without clear user consent
organizations: Koko (Kokobot peer-support service)
what_happened: In January 2023 Koko co-founder Rob Morris said about 4,000 people received peer-support replies at least partly written by GPT-3. Recipients saw only a note saying the reply was written in collaboration with Koko Bot, and the only way to opt out was not to read it. Morris said users rated co-written replies higher but that the benefit disappeared once people learned a machine was involved. Academics and journalists criticized the experiment as testing on vulnerable people without informed consent.
failure_mechanism: AI involvement was disclosed vaguely and without an opt-out to people seeking emotional support, and the experiment had no independent ethics review.
lesson_for_builders: Tell users plainly when AI wrote or helped write a message, and get independent ethics review before experimenting on people seeking mental-health support.
sources: NBC News, Jan 2023
notes: Facts about the experiment come from the founder's own statements as reported; Morris said it was a product feature, not a study, and that Koko had no federal funding so IRB review was not legally required. Accounts of the experiment's details varied between the original thread and later clarifications. No regulator action found.

title: Crisis hotline shared anonymized conversation data with a for-profit spinoff
organizations: Crisis Text Line; Loris.ai
what_happened: In January 2022 Politico reported that Crisis Text Line shared anonymized texters' conversation data with Loris.ai, a for-profit customer-service software company spun off by its founder, in which Crisis Text Line held an ownership stake. Crisis Text Line said the data was scrubbed of personally identifiable information and that the relationship was public; privacy experts questioned whether it could be truly anonymous and whether users understood. After criticism, including a request from an FCC commissioner, it ended the arrangement on 31 January 2022 and asked Loris to delete the data.
failure_mechanism: Sensitive mental-health conversations were reused commercially in a way users did not clearly expect, relying on anonymization and broad consent.
lesson_for_builders: Do not assume anonymization or buried consent covers commercial reuse of mental-health data; ask what a user in crisis would expect.
outcome: Crisis Text Line ended the data sharing and asked Loris to delete the data.
sources: Popular Science, Feb 2022 (summarizing Politico's reporting)
notes: No regulator finding of wrongdoing was found. Whether the data could be re-identified was questioned by experts but not shown. The Politico original was not fetched.

title: Hospital gave 1.6 million patient records to DeepMind for a kidney-injury app trial
organizations: Royal Free London NHS Foundation Trust; Google DeepMind; UK Information Commissioner's Office
what_happened: The UK Information Commissioner's Office found in July 2017 that the Royal Free NHS Foundation Trust broke the Data Protection Act when it provided 1.6 million patient records to Google DeepMind for a trial of an acute kidney injury alert and detection system. Patients were not adequately told, and the Commissioner said they would not reasonably have expected this use. The Trust signed an undertaking to establish a legal basis, complete a privacy impact assessment, and commission an audit.
failure_mechanism: Identifiable records for all patients were shared to develop and test an app without a proper legal basis, transparency, or a prior privacy impact assessment.
lesson_for_builders: Establish the legal basis and notice for any data you use to develop or test a tool before data moves, and use only the data you need.
outcome: No fine; the Trust signed an undertaking. The Trust accepted the findings and DeepMind welcomed the resolution.
sources: The Register, 3 Jul 2017 (summarizing the ICO decision)
notes: UK law (Data Protection Act 1998, since replaced), not US. The ICO's own decision page returned 404, so a news summary was used. DeepMind stated it underestimated the complexity of NHS rules (seen in search snippets only).

title: FTC action over telehealth counseling data shared for advertising
organizations: BetterHelp; Federal Trade Commission
what_happened: In March 2023 the FTC announced that online counseling service BetterHelp had disclosed consumers' email addresses, IP addresses, and health questionnaire answers to Facebook, Snapchat, Criteo, and Pinterest for advertising despite promising to keep the data private. The FTC said BetterHelp did not obtain affirmative express consent. The order requires $7.8 million for partial refunds and bans sharing health data for advertising.
failure_mechanism: Sensitive health information from an intake form flowed to advertising platforms contrary to the company's privacy promises.
lesson_for_builders: Audit every third-party SDK, pixel, and analytics tool on health intake flows, and make privacy statements match what the product actually does.
outcome: Proposed order announced 2 March 2023 and, per search results, finalized in July 2023 by a 3-0 Commission vote.
sources: FTC press release, 2 Mar 2023
notes: Not an AI failure; included because it illustrates secondary use of health data outside HIPAA. The final-order release was seen only in search results, so the finalization date is not fetched-confirmed. Whether BetterHelp admitted or denied the allegations is not stated in the fetched release. BetterHelp's response is not in the release.

title: Court held Idaho's automated Medicaid budget cuts violated due process
organizations: Idaho Department of Health and Welfare; ACLU of Idaho (counsel for plaintiffs)
what_happened: In K.W. v. Armstrong, a class of about 4,000 Idahoans with developmental disabilities challenged cuts to their Medicaid assistance set by the state's decision formulas. In March 2016 Chief Judge Winmill held, per the ACLU's release, that the department arbitrarily deprived participants of property rights and violated due process, and ordered testing of the reliability and accuracy of its automated systems. The department had called its formulas trade secrets and declined to disclose the reasons for the cuts.
failure_mechanism: Coverage amounts were set by an opaque automated formula, with no meaningful notice, explanation, or way for people to challenge the result.
lesson_for_builders: If a tool sets benefits or coverage, give affected people the basis for the result and a real way to contest it.
outcome: Court-ordered remedies including testing of the automated systems; an earlier injunction restoring about $30 million a year was upheld by the Ninth Circuit in 2015, per the ACLU.
sources: ACLU press release, 30 Mar 2016
notes: Replacement for the dropped eGFR candidate. The ruling quote comes through the plaintiffs' counsel's release, not the opinion itself; the tool is a benefits formula, not a modern ML model, so it qualifies only as a mechanism example (opaque automated decisions with no effective challenge). The state's response was not found.

title: Experimental resume-screening model learned to penalize women
organizations: Amazon
what_happened: Reuters reported in October 2018 that Amazon had built an experimental machine-learning resume-rating tool trained on about ten years of submitted resumes, mostly from men. The tool penalized resumes containing the word women's and downgraded graduates of two all-women's colleges. Amazon edited it to neutralize those terms but could not guarantee it would not find other discriminatory patterns, and the team was disbanded by early 2017.
failure_mechanism: The model learned from historical hiring outcomes that reflected a male-dominated workforce, so the past decisions became the target.
lesson_for_builders: When the label is past human decisions, test for and expect the model to reproduce past bias, including through proxies you cannot list.
outcome: Project abandoned; Reuters reported a watered-down version was used for rudimentary tasks.
sources: Reuters via Business Insurance, Oct 2018
notes: Relies on anonymous sources. Reuters said recruiters looked at the rankings but did not rely solely on them; Amazon declined to comment on the engine. A search snippet says Amazon told another outlet the tool was never used to evaluate candidates, which conflicts with that account and is why the status is mixed.

title: Recidivism risk scores had different error rates for Black and white defendants
organizations: Northpointe (now Equivant); ProPublica
what_happened: A 2016 ProPublica analysis of COMPAS risk scores in Broward County, Florida found that Black defendants who did not reoffend were labeled higher risk 44.9% of the time versus 23.5% for white defendants, while white defendants who did reoffend were labeled lower risk more often (47.7% versus 28.0%). ProPublica also reported only 20% of people predicted to commit violent crimes did so. Northpointe said it does not agree with the analysis and defended the test's accuracy.
failure_mechanism: Error rates diverged by race even though the score was built to predict rearrest, a stand-in for reoffending.
lesson_for_builders: Report error rates by subgroup and decide in advance which fairness criterion matters for your use, since they cannot all hold when base rates differ.
sources: ProPublica, 'Machine Bias', 23 May 2016
notes: Disputed: Northpointe and later academic work argued the scores were equally accurate across groups (predictive parity) and that the fairness measures conflict; those rebuttals were not fetched. The arrest-as-outcome point in failure_mechanism is general background, not from the fetched article.

title: Dutch tax authority fined for using nationality in fraud risk selection
organizations: Dutch Tax and Customs Administration; Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP)
what_happened: In December 2021 the Dutch Data Protection Authority fined the Tax and Customs Administration EUR 2.75 million for unlawfully processing the nationality data of childcare benefit applicants, including using dual nationality as a risk indicator in its risk classification model although the law says it should not play a part. The data should have been deleted in 2014, but nationality data on 1.4 million people was still registered in 2018. The wider childcare benefits scandal, in which thousands of families had benefits stopped and were ordered to repay, led to the Dutch cabinet's resignation in January 2021.
failure_mechanism: A protected characteristic or its proxy was used as an input to a risk model that selected people for fraud investigation, with severe consequences and little recourse.
lesson_for_builders: Do not use protected characteristics or close proxies as inputs for decisions that affect people's benefits or care, and audit selection rates by group.
outcome: EUR 2.75 million fine, which the junior finance minister said the government would aim to pay by year end; compensation payments to affected families (about 15,000 people had received EUR 30,000 per DutchNews).
sources: Pinsent Masons Out-Law, 13 Dec 2021; DutchNews, 8 Dec 2021
notes: The AP's own decision was not fetched; news summaries were used. DutchNews gives the fine as 2.7 million, Pinsent Masons as 2.75 million (the latter used). Other reports describe the model as self-learning and the number of wrongly accused families as about 26,000; neither fetched article says so, so they are omitted.

title: Australian automated welfare debt recovery found unlawful by Royal Commission
organizations: Australian Department of Human Services (Services Australia); Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme
what_happened: Australia's Robodebt scheme automatically calculated welfare overpayments by averaging annual income across pay periods. The Royal Commission's final report of 7 July 2023 found that the scheme produced inaccurate results and did not comply with the income calculation provisions of the Social Security Act. After a 2020 class action settled, debts raised through averaging were reduced to zero, and a Minister said 443,000 people were identified in the Federal Court proceedings.
failure_mechanism: An automated rule applied an invalid shortcut (income averaging) to raise debts at scale, shifting the burden to individuals to disprove them with little human review.
lesson_for_builders: Validate that an automated rule is lawful and accurate before scaling, and keep a human review and a low-friction challenge path.
outcome: Debts raised through averaging were reduced to zero after a 2020 class action settlement; the Royal Commission made recommendations including more oversight of automated decision-making.
sources: APRA copy of an overview of the Royal Commission final report; ABC News, 7 Jul 2023; The Conversation, income averaging explainer
notes: Rule-based automation, not machine learning; it qualifies as a mechanism example of automated decisions without human review. The Royal Commission's own site timed out, so a regulator-hosted overview and news coverage were used. Debt totals vary by source (A$1.73 to 1.8 billion) and are not stated in what_happened.

title: Michigan unemployment fraud system falsely accused thousands without human review
organizations: Michigan Unemployment Insurance Agency
what_happened: Michigan's MiDAS system, in use from October 2013, made fraud determinations without human involvement until August 2015. The agency acknowledged it falsely accused at least 20,000 residents of fraud, and Detroit Free Press records requests pointed to a 93% error rate. A class action settled for $20 million, with final approval in January 2024; the state acknowledged it had not required a human to check the computer's conclusions and had automatically assessed large fines and penalties.
failure_mechanism: Fraud findings and penalties were issued automatically with a data problem and no human check, and claimants who did not respond to a questionnaire could be defaulted into a finding.
lesson_for_builders: Do not let a model finalize adverse decisions on its own, and measure its error rate on a sample before and after launch.
trigger_rule: autonomy_high AND automated_significant_decision AND (utilization_review OR org_government)
outcome: $20 million class settlement approved January 2024; the agency still uses MiDAS but requires human verification of fraud determinations.
sources: Bridge Michigan on the settlement; GovTech on the Detroit Free Press 93% error-rate reporting
notes: The 93% figure is press-reported and its calculation is not explained in the fetched article. The questionnaire-default detail comes from a search snippet, not a fetched page. Rule-based system, not machine learning. Year 2016 is when the problem became widely public; the agency review dates are not confirmed in fetched sources.

title: Airline held liable for its website chatbot's wrong refund advice
organizations: Air Canada; British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal
what_happened: In Moffatt v. Air Canada (2024 BCCRT 149), a customer relied on the airline's website chatbot, which said he could apply for a bereavement fare within 90 days after buying his ticket; Air Canada's policy did not allow retroactive requests. Air Canada argued the chatbot was a separate legal entity responsible for its own actions. The tribunal rejected that, held the chatbot was part of the airline's website, and found Air Canada liable for negligent misrepresentation.
failure_mechanism: A customer-facing chatbot stated a policy incorrectly, and the company had not taken care to ensure the chatbot was accurate.
lesson_for_builders: You are responsible for what your patient-facing chatbot says, so test it against your actual policies and show the authoritative source.
outcome: Air Canada was ordered to pay damages of about C$650 plus interest and fees, reported as just over C$800 in total.
sources: Hull & Hull summary of Moffatt v. Air Canada; EH Law summary of Moffatt v. Air Canada
notes: A small-claims tribunal decision, not a court of general jurisdiction. The decision text on CanLII and the tribunal site was blocked (403), so law-firm summaries were used; the decision date (14 Feb 2024 per a search result) is not stated in the row. Law-firm summaries state the amounts slightly differently (C$650.88 damages; over C$800 total).

title: Lawyers sanctioned after filing fake case citations generated by ChatGPT
organizations: Levidow, Levidow & Oberman; US District Court, S.D.N.Y.
what_happened: In Mata v. Avianca, two lawyers filed a brief citing non-existent judicial opinions generated by ChatGPT, with fabricated quotes and citations, and continued to defend them after the court questioned their existence. On 22 June 2023 Judge P. Kevin Castel imposed a $5,000 penalty on the lawyers and their firm and ordered them to notify their client and each judge falsely named as an author. He said using AI is not inherently improper but lawyers have a gatekeeping duty to ensure accuracy.
failure_mechanism: A generative model produced plausible but fabricated citations, and the users did not verify them against primary sources.
lesson_for_builders: Make AI-cited sources verifiable in one click and design review so users check them, because users will otherwise trust fluent citations.
outcome: $5,000 sanction and notification requirements imposed on the attorneys and firm.
sources: LawNext, 22 Jun 2023 (summarizing the sanctions opinion)
notes: The sanctions opinion itself was not fetched (CourtListener search did not return it); a legal-news summary was used. The court also found bad faith based on the lawyers' later statements.

title: Engineers uploaded internal source code to a public chatbot
organizations: Samsung Electronics
what_happened: In May 2023 Bloomberg reported on an internal Samsung memo stating that engineers had accidentally leaked internal source code by uploading it to ChatGPT in April. Samsung told staff in a key division not to use generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, describing the restriction as temporary, because data sent to external servers is hard to retrieve or delete and could be accessible to other users. The memo warned that violations could lead to termination.
failure_mechanism: Staff pasted confidential material into a consumer AI service whose data handling the company did not control.
lesson_for_builders: Give staff an approved, contractually protected AI tool and block consumer ones for patient data, rather than relying on a policy alone.
outcome: Temporary restriction on generative AI tools in the affected division while Samsung worked on a secure environment.
sources: CSO Online, 2 May 2023 (reporting on Bloomberg's review of the memo)
notes: Source is the company's own memo as reported; the memo did not say what the code was or whether anyone outside Samsung saw it. Source code, not health data, but the same behavior.

title: Self-driving test fatality linked to operator automation complacency
organizations: Uber Advanced Technologies Group; National Transportation Safety Board
what_happened: The NTSB investigated a March 2018 crash in Tempe, Arizona, in which an Uber ATG test vehicle under automated control struck and killed a pedestrian. It found the probable cause was the vehicle operator's failure to monitor the driving environment and the automated system because she was visually distracted by her phone. Contributing factors included Uber ATG's lack of adequate mechanisms for addressing operators' automation complacency, ineffective oversight of operators, inadequate safety risk assessment, and an inadequate safety culture.
failure_mechanism: The design relied on a human monitor to catch failures of an automated system but did not address the predictable drop in attention during long periods of monitoring.
lesson_for_builders: If your safety case depends on a human catching errors, test whether they actually do, and add countermeasures for complacency.
sources: NTSB investigation page HWY18MH010 (report HAR-19-03)
notes: NTSB report HAR-19-03; the investigation page states the pedestrian died (checked 2026-10-12). The pedestrian crossing outside a crosswalk was also a contributing factor.

title: UK exam grading model abandoned after public backlash
organizations: Ofqual (England's qualifications regulator)
what_happened: In summer 2020, with exams cancelled, Ofqual used a statistical standardisation model to produce calculated grades alongside teachers' centre assessment grades. After concerns grew following A level results day, Ofqual's board decided to award students the higher of the centre assessment grade or the calculated grade. Ofqual's 2020-21 annual report said the approach had a detrimental impact on public trust and confidence, and its Chair publicly apologised.
failure_mechanism: Individual outcomes were set by a group-level statistical model with no easy individual challenge, which eroded trust in fairness.
lesson_for_builders: Give individuals a way to contest model-driven outcomes and check outcomes by group before release.
outcome: Grades were reverted to the higher of teacher or calculated grades in August 2020.
sources: Ofqual Annual Report and Accounts 2020-21; Ofqual, 26 Nov 2020, summer 2020 outcomes analysis
notes: Mixed: Ofqual acknowledged the loss of public confidence, but its November 2020 analysis found students were not systemically disadvantaged by protected characteristic or socioeconomic status; this was disputed publicly. The 'group-level model, no easy individual challenge' mechanism and how the model used schools' past results are background not confirmed in the fetched pages, and downgrade percentages (about 40%) came from search snippets and are not used.
